editorial_excerpt_zh: 作为以大地艺术先驱闻名的常驻纽约艺术家艾伦·索恩费斯特在日本的首场个展。作为从六本木迁至东日本桥的画廊搬迁后的首场展览，本展将介绍在其时代艺术、文化及土地风景拼贴于濒危动植物轮廓之中的系列作品。 The post アラン・ソンフィスト「Echoes of a Vanishing World」 @ Yumiko Chiba Associates first appeared on ART iT（アートイット） .

article_text:
アラン・ソンフィスト「Echoes of a Vanishing World」 2026年10月17日（土）–12月5日（土） Yumiko Chiba Associates（東京都中央区東日本橋2-22-1 クロスシー東日本橋ビル 1F） https://www.ycassociates.co.jp/ 開廊時間：12:00–19:00 休廊日：日、月、祝 展覧会URL： https://ycassociates.co.jp/exhibitions/2026/10/13/2979/

Yumiko Chiba Associatesでは、ランド・アートの先駆者として知られるニューヨーク拠点のアーティスト、アラン・ソンフィストの個展「Echoes of a Vanishing World」を開催する。六本木から東日本橋に移転した同ギャラリーの移転後初の展覧会であり、ソンフィストにとっては日本で初めての個展となる。 アラン・ソンフィスト （1946年アメリカ・ニューヨーク生まれ）は、ニューヨークを拠点に、1960年代から半世紀以上にわたり、芸術を地球環境やエコロジカルな視点へと拡張しようとしてきた。その活動を象徴する作品に、都市開発で失われたマンハッタンの森を在来の植物だけで再現した《タイム・ランドスケープ》（1965–現在）がある。1976年のヴェネツィア・ビエンナーレ、1977年のドクメンタ6に参加したほか、1970年代から1980年代にはレオ・カステリ・ギャラリーおよびマリアン・グッドマン・ギャラリー（いずれもニューヨーク）で複数回の個展を開催。2012年には、ロサンゼルス現代美術館（MOCA）とミュンヘンのハウス・デア・クンストで開催された「Ends of the Earth: Land Art to 1974」にサイトスペシフィック作品を出品した。近年の主な展覧会に「Celestial Landscape」（パリッシュ・アート・ミュージアム、サウサンプトン、アメリカ、2026）、「Seeds of Time – Retrospective of Alan Sonfist」（パルコ・アルテ・ヴィヴェンテ、トリノ、イタリア、2025）、「Microorganism Landscapes」（ミラノ・トリエンナーレ、2025）、「Burning Forest」（ローリー現代美術館、アメリカ、2024）、「Nature is Art」（ミュージアム・ウェーブ、ソウル、2023）などがある。2023年には団体Land Art Forwardを設立し、アーティスト、科学者、市民が協働して環境芸術プロジェクトを生み出すことを目指している。作品はニューヨーク近代美術館（MoMA）、ホイットニー美術館、メトロポリタン美術館、ソロモン・R・グッゲンハイム美術館などに収蔵されている。

本展では、ソンフィストが2000年代から開始したシリーズ〈Echoes of a Vanishing World（消えゆく世界の残響）〉を紹介する。本シリーズは、絶滅危惧種の動物・植物を選び、その動植物の輪郭のなかに、その時代の芸術・文化や、彼らが生存していたであろう土地の風景などをコラージュした作品からなる。「私は自分の作品で大地を改変するのではなく、取り戻したいのです」と 語る ソンフィストは、自然や動植物を人間の世界と切り離されたものではなく、ともに生きる存在として捉え、本シリーズの作品を、環境や文化を伝える生きたアーカイヴとして提示する。 なお、Yumiko Chiba Associatesは移転を機に、ゲストキュレーターを迎えて年に一度、所属作家に限定せずに企画する新シリーズ「VERBS」をスタートする。毎回ひとつの動詞をテーマに設定し、1〜3名のアーティストの作品を通じて、その動詞について考え、議論する場をつくる企画で、コンセプターおよび初回ゲストキュレーターは文化研究者の 山本浩貴 が務める。また、芸術的／批評的な議論の拠点となるプログラムとして2022年に始まった「六本木アルスクーリア」は、「東日本橋アルスクーリア」と名を改めて継続する。2011年から「批評をアーカイヴする」というコンセプトのもとに編纂してきた研究冊子『クリティカル・アーカイヴ』をはじめとする出版活動も続けていく。

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在公众的想象中，“哥特”一词让人联想到天鹅绒斗篷、斑驳的城堡以及蝙蝠洞（Batcave）里身穿黑衣的年轻人。这怎么可能与唐·麦库林（Don McCullin）拍摄的康赛特（Consett）钢铁厂，或者1969年8月阿基彦·冈村（Akihiko Okamura）镜头下战火中的德里（Derry）街头有什么共同之处？“暗黑故事：英国纪实摄影与哥特风”（Dark Tales: British Documentary Photography and the Gothic）策展人艾萨克·布利斯（Isaac Blease）回答说：一切皆有。“自诞生之日起，摄影便是一种用于记录那些令现代世界感到动荡不安的动荡、政治、道德和社会议题的媒介，”他观察到，“某种黑暗在其历史中潜滋暗长。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": Jones）在去工业化低谷期的1962年拍摄的一张照片。花盘上摆着的一片烤番茄配吐司，看起来像是一个张开的伤口。人们可能会把这张照片归功于马丁·帕尔（Martin Parr）；但它的署名是安娜·福克斯（Anna Fox），一位英国日常生活与乡村生活的敏锐观察者。福克斯的系列作品《来自家园的便条》（Notes from Home）中的“皮特的食物与鲜花”（Pete’s Food and article_text:
In the popular imagination, the word “Gothic” summons velvet capes, crumbling castles, black-clad teenagers at the Batcave. What could it possibly share with Don McCullin photographing the steelworks of Consett, or Akihiko Okamura in the burning streets of Derry in August 1969? Everything, answers Isaac Blease, curator of “Dark Tales: British Documentary Photography and the Gothic.” “From its inception, photography has been a medium used to record the troubled, political, moral and social issues that have unsettled the modern world,” he observes. “A certain darkness creeps throughout its histories.”

On the muddy ground of England’s industrial north, a woman strides past, pushing her pram beneath a sky devoured by the black smoke of a steelworks. The great photojournalist Don McCullin caught this scene in Consett in 1974. Within a single frame, the dawn of one life brushes against the dusk of an industry. Like penitents on the Stations of the Cross, the men and women of Sunderland kneel on a slag heap, scavenging for something to keep themselves warm, in an image made by Colin Jones in 1962, at the depths of deindustrialization. A grilled tomato on toast, set on a flowered plate, resembles an open wound. One might have ascribed this picture to Martin Parr; it is signed Anna Fox, a keen observer of English domestic and rural life. Drawn from Notes from Home, Fox’s series “Pete’s Food and Flowers” chronicles the daily life of Pete, a former soldier suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder whom she had taken into her home in Selborne, Hampshire. In her images, a seemingly ordinary kitchen becomes the silent theater of an invisible violence.

Such pictures issue from decades of social documentary photography, carried by generations of image-makers determined to bear witness to British reality, from the working class to political conflict, from domestic interiors to industrial landscapes in ruin. And yet something rumbles within them, something that feels like terror. This is precisely what the exhibition lays bare: beneath the documentary gaze, the Gothic surfaces. For both traditions share a founding conviction: horror dwells in the familiar. The show unfolds across four enigmatically titled chapters, The Castle, Domestic Bliss, Double Take, and Night Creatures, which function, in Blease’s words, “almost like a series of short tales.”

In The Castle, the British documentarian Janine Wiedel and the Swede Kjell-Åke Andersson, whose work was forged in the heart of British heavy industry, photograph molten steel and silhouettes dissolved into shadow within the gloom of the foundries. Double Take plays on appearances: here Chris Shaw photographs Jordi the Lounge Lizzard, a man in a braided uniform sprawled across the baroque sofa of a London hotel, laid out to the eye like a figure in his padded coffin. A portraitist of the London underground scene, Derek Ridgers photographs, in the chapter Night Creatures, the regulars of the Batcave, a Soho nightclub now vanished, which was one of the birthplaces of British Goth culture.

Among the most unsettling works is Sarah Pickering’s. Her series “Incident,” made during a residency at the UK Fire Service College between 2006 and 2007, documents entirely fabricated interiors: sets built for arson-investigation training exercises, repeatedly set ablaze and then pored over in their ashes. A Boots logo, the best-known pharmacy chain in Britain, floats above an empty shop. The photographer prints her work in large format on matte fibre paper, “giving the blacks and print surface an almost ashy quality,” notes Blease, with “a powerful sense of suspense and tension.”

Great names from elsewhere, Robert Frank, Lee Miller, and Akihiko Okamura, are summoned too into this wholly British story. “Photographic culture here has always relied on a crossing over between different cultures and ideas,” Blease recalls, citing the affinities of Bill Brandt and Lee Miller with the Surrealists. “The natural and social conditions of Britain,” he adds, “often lead to something that has Gothic connotations,” from the weather to the architecture, from the brooding landscapes to the scars of industry.

“Darkroom processing is inherently Gothic in the way that it memorializes,” Blease asserts. The whole exhibition partakes of this logic, funereal and alive at once, summoning the dead to speak to the living, at a moment when documentary itself is passing through a shadow, its purpose and legitimacy in question, undermined by public distrust of photographers. And artificial intelligence above all, whose threat the curator judges nothing less than “existential.”

“Dark Tales: British Documentary Photography and the Gothic” is part of the 2026 Bristol Photo Festival and is on view at the Martin Parr Foundation , Bristol, through December 20, 2026. Admission free.

Elizabeth II）、西班牙国王、黛安娜王妃（Princess Diana）、摩纳哥的格蕾丝王妃（Princess Grace）和卡罗琳公主（Princess Caroline）、安迪·沃霍尔（Andy Warhol）、穆罕默德·阿里（Mohammed Ali）、马丁·路德·金博士（Dr. Martin Luther King），以及滚石乐队（The Rolling Stones）、谁人乐队（The Who）、葛丽泰·嘉宝（Greta Garbo）、弗兰克·辛纳屈（Frank Sinatra）、伊丽莎白·泰勒（Elizabeth Taylor）、杰克·尼科尔森（Jack Nicholson）、艾米·怀恩豪斯（Amy Winehouse）和布拉德·皮特（Brad Pitt）等演艺界名流。本森还报道过海湾战争、波斯尼亚战争、阿富汗战争，诸如此类，不胜枚举。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2009年，本森因对摄影事业的贡献被英国女王伊丽莎白二世授予大英帝国司令勋章（CBE）。他曾两次被评为美国国家新闻摄影师协会（NPPA）年度杂志摄影师，并两次荣获徕卡卓越奖（Leica Medal of Excellence）。2013年，哈里被苏格兰圣安德鲁斯大学授予荣誉文学博士学位，此前他于2009年获得格拉斯哥大学和格拉斯哥艺术学院的荣誉文学博士学位，随后还被伦敦皇家摄影学会授予荣誉会士。本森的照片被华盛顿特区的史密森尼国家肖像馆、格拉斯哥的 Kelvingrove 博物馆以及爱丁堡的国家肖像馆作为永久馆藏收藏。他作为战地摄影记者的60年职业生涯包括与《生活》杂志（LIFE Magazine）的长期合同，其作品曾登上全球各大主流杂志的封面及内页，包括：《Life》、《Time》、《Newsweek》、《Town & Country》、《Vanity Fair》、《G.Q.》、《Esquire》、《W》、《The London Sunday Times》、《People》、《Vogue》和《Architectural Digest》。他举办过40场个人摄影展，出版了17本书籍，其中最新的是由塔森出版社（Taschen）于2013年出版的《The Beatles On the Road: 1964-1966》。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "萨拉·塔西尼（Sara Tasini）：2009年，您被伊丽莎白女王授予大英帝国司令勋章（CBE），这是一项极高的荣誉。2007年，您又获得了家乡格拉斯哥大学授予的荣誉博士学位。您刚刚结束苏格兰之行，在那里您又获得了一项声誉卓著的奖项。能告诉我是为了什么奖吗？您的这趟行程怎么样？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈里·本森：2013年6月，我获得了圣安德鲁斯大学颁发的荣誉文学博士学位。我开始职业生涯时并没有期望获得任何奖项，但在我做了60年自己热爱的事情——拍照之后——能够获得这些荣誉，我深感荣幸。如果当年我在格拉斯哥伊斯特伍德中学（Eastwood Secondary School）的同班同学打赌看谁会是最后一个拿到博士学位的人，我肯定会稳操胜券。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是什么最初吸引您走上摄影之路，又是什么一直让您坚持到现在？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "可能是我的父亲。也可能是在战争中长大的经历，伴随着那个时代的狂热，让我想要成为其中的一部分。在收音机里听温斯顿·丘吉尔爵士的演讲，让我渴望去探寻世界上正在发生的事情的核心。而且我在报纸上看到的照片也鼓励我去成为其中的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "摄影是最容易让你保持动力的事情。相机基本上会按你的意愿去做任何事。其中有一种纯粹与兴奋；它不需要那么复杂。你可以自行判断什么是好照片，什么是坏照片——不要听取任何其他人的意见——关键在于你喜欢什么。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "您觉得您对摄影的这种天赋是从何而来的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我从未接受过任何培训，但我并不是说这是件坏事。我认为我在伦敦舰队街（Fleet Street）工作时学到了很多东西。当时至少有10家日报，每一家都在为早报的独家新闻而竞争。那种竞争意识至今没有离开我。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "人们认为您与披头士乐队的合作开启了您的国际职业生涯。您同意这种说法吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不同意。我和披头士乐队只在一起待了三 weeks（注：原文为three weeks，保留英文或译为三周，按数字规则保留），后来也只是断断续续合作了两年。在那之后，我直接投入了硬新闻报道：种族骚乱、马丁·路德·金、越南战争、爱尔兰共和军（IRA），以及各行各业的人。但话虽如此，我很高兴自己拍摄了披头士乐队，因为我拍摄的可以说是上个世纪最伟大的音乐创作者。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "您是如何能够与世界上许多最著名的人物建立如此深入而密切的联系的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为《生活》杂志（LIFE）工作在其中起了很大作用。在60年代和70年代，它是人人都想为其工作、人人都想登上其页面的首要杂志。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "面对如此庞大的作品集，您能够挑出自己最喜欢的照片，或者对您最有意义的照片吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "嗯，你总会有自己偏爱的一些照片。我的首选可能是罗伯特·肯尼迪遇刺案和披头士枕头大战（Beatles Pillow Fight）。我还要加上杜鲁门·卡波特（Truman Capote）的黑白舞会（Black and White Ball）、国际象棋冠军鲍比·费舍尔（Bobby Fischer），以及我为安迪·沃霍尔拍摄的照片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "您最喜欢拍摄的主题是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一则好的新闻故事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "拍摄某些悲惨事件（例如1968年罗伯特·肯尼迪遇刺案）时，在如此之多的混乱和创伤中，你是如何设法保持专注去拍摄照片的？这是否需要一定程度的情感疏离？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我当时一直告诫自己：“这是为了历史，今天可别搞砸了，明天再砸。”我一直都能够把情绪抽离出来。我的职责是获取照片并把工作做好。我的工作不是对事件产生情绪波动。我认识罗伯特·肯尼迪，我很喜欢他，但我的工作是为历史记录下正在发生的事情，我知道他会理解这一点的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "轻松一点的话题，你对数字彩色摄影的创作让我非常感兴趣。彩色摄影能为你提供黑白摄影无法企及的东西吗？反之亦然吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "现在我只用数字彩色拍摄，它可以转换成黑白，但我很高兴我早期的职业生涯是用胶片完成的，大多是黑白胶片。当我与画廊的人以及街上的人交流时，他们总是说他们更喜欢黑白。黑白一直是摄影师的媒介，而彩色则是画家的媒介。话虽如此，当杂志要求封面、名人等内容使用彩色时，我一直都在用彩色拍摄。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着互联网、社交媒体的出现，以及现代视觉影像几乎可以即时捕捉和传播，摄影记者的工作发生了怎样的变化？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "现在任何拿着手机的人都可以成为摄影师。这很惊人，但这并没有让摄影变得更好。由于速度变快了，它反而变糟了。一分钟拍上百张照片或者诸如此类的操作，并不一定能带来好的摄影作品。对我来说，当今的数字彩色战争照片不如用胶片拍摄的战争照片引人入胜，这很有意思，因为你可以回头看越南战争和二战的照片——所有数字时代之前的照片，在我看来它们就是更好。这只是我的个人意见，别人肯定会有不同看法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当人们看你的照片时，你希望他们欣赏到什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我只希望他们喜欢，这就够了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这次采访是总部位于佛罗里达州棕榈滩的霍尔登·兰茨画廊（Holden Luntz Gallery）系列采访的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "采访者：萨拉·塔西尼（Sara Tasini）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Holden Luntz Gallery 332 Worth Ave Palm Beach, FL 33480 USA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "http://www.holdenluntz.com/", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Archives – October 27, 2016

Harry Benson was born in Glasgow amid the drama of WWII with bombs dropping overhead, but Benson managed to escape through the lens of a camera. His curious fortune struck when he was given a particular assignment in 1964: to capture The Beatles in France and on their first journey to the United States. This experience not only made for some of the most famous Beatles photography, but also sent Benson’s life in a completely new direction. During the civil war in the Dominican Republic, both sides captured Benson in one day. He caught the horror on Ethel Kennedy’s face in the Ambassador Hotel after her husband Senator Robert Kennedy had been shot. Harry has photographed an amazing range of subjects including eleven US presidents and their families from Eisenhower to Obama. Portraits of major forces of the last half of the 20th century include Sir Winston Churchill, HRH Queen Elizabeth II, The King of Spain, Princess Diana, Princess Grace and Princess Caroline of Monaco, Andy Warhol, Mohammed Ali, Dr. Martin Luther King and entertainers The Rolling Stones, The Who, Greta Garbo, Frank Sinatra, Elizabeth Taylor, Jack Nicholson, Amy Winehouse and Brad Pitt. Benson covered wars in the Gulf, Bosnia, Afghanistan, and the list goes on.

In 2009, Benson was named Commander of the Order of the British Empire, (CBE) by HRH Queen Elizabeth for his service to photography. He was twice named NPPA Magazine Photographer of the Year and was twice awarded the Leica Medal of Excellence. In 2013 Harry received an honorary Doctor of Letters from the University of St. Andrews, Scotland, and in 2009 an honorary Doctor of Letters from Glasgow University and the Glasgow School of Art followed by an Honorary Fellow of the Royal Photographic Society in London. Benson’s photographs are in the permanent collection of the Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery in Washington, D.C.; Kelvingrove Museum in Glasgow and the National Portrait Gallery in Edinburgh. His 60-year career as a photojournalist included a contract with LIFE Magazine and photographs on the covers and inside major magazines worldwide, including: Life, Time, Newsweek, Town & Country, Vanity Fair, G.Q., Esquire, W, The London Sunday Times, People, Vogue, and Architectural Digest. He has enjoyed 40 solo exhibitions and published 17 books including most recently, “The Beatles On the Road: 1964-1966” published by Taschen in 2013.

Sara Tasini: In 2009 you were made a CBE, a Commander of the Order of the British Empire by Queen Elizabeth, which is a tremendous honor. And in 2007 you received an honorary doctorate from Glasgow University, your hometown. You just returned from a trip to Scotland, where you received another prestigious award. Can you tell me what it was for? And how was your trip?

Harry Benson: In June 2013 I received an honorary degree of Doctor of Letters from the University of St. Andrews. I didn’t start my career expecting any awards, but I am very honored to receive them after 60 years of doing what I love to do – taking photographs. If there had been a bet made by my classmates at Eastwood Secondary School in Glasgow about who would be the last person to receive a doctorate, I would have won, hands down.

What first drew you to photography and what keeps you there?

It could have been my father. It could also have been growing up during the war with the excitement of the time, wanting to be part of something. Listening to Sir Winston Churchill’s speeches on the radio made me want to get to the center of what was happening in the world. And I would see photographs in the newspaper that would encourage me to be part of it.

Photography is the easiest thing to keep you motivated. The camera will basically do whatever you want it to do. There is a simplicity and excitement; it doesn’t have to be complicated. You can judge what’s a good picture, what’s a bad picture – don’t take anybody else’s opinion – it’s what you like.

From where do you think your natural ability for photography comes?

I never had any training, but I’m not saying that’s a bad thing. I think I learned a lot while working on London’s Fleet Street. There were at least 10 daily newspapers and each was trying to scoop the others for the morning edition. That sense of competitiveness has not left me.

Your work with the Beatles is thought to have launched your international career. Would you agree with this statement?

I wouldn’t agree. I was only with the Beatles for three weeks and then off and on for two years. Afterward I went straight to hard news stories: race riots, MLK, Vietnam, the IRA, people from all walks of life. But with that said, I am glad I photographed the Beatles because I photographed arguably the greatest musical composers of the last century.

How were you able to get so involved and so in depth with many of the most famous people in the world?

Working for LIFE magazine had a lot to do with it. In the 60’s and 70’s it was the premiere magazine that everyone wanted to work for and everyone wanted to be in.

With such a substantial portfolio, are you able to pick out pictures that are your favorites or have any that are most meaningful to you?

Well you’ve got your favorites. Mine would probably be the Bobby Kennedy assassination and the Beatles Pillow Fight. I would also add Truman Capote’s Black and White Ball, chess champion Bobby Fischer, and the photographs I have taken of Andy Warhol.

What is your favorite subject to photograph?

A good news story.

Photographing certain tragic events, for instance the assassination of Robert Kennedy in 1968, how do you manage to remain focused on getting the picture in the midst of so much chaos and trauma? Does it require a certain amount of emotional detachment?

I kept thinking ‘this is for history, don’t mess up today, mess up tomorrow.’ I’ve always been able to cut myself off. My business is to get photographs and do my job well. My job is not to get emotional about it. I knew Bobby Kennedy, I liked him very much, but my job was to document what was happening for history, and I know he would understand that.

On a lighter note, your work in digital color interests me very much. Is there something color photography could offer you that black and white couldn’t? And vice versa?

Now I only work in digital color which can be converted to black and white, but I’m glad my earlier career was done on film , mostly in black and white. When I speak to people in galleries and on the street they invariably say they prefer black and white. Black and white has always been the medium of the photographer and color has been for painters. That said, I have always worked in color when magazines asked for it for covers, for celebrities, etc.

With the advent of the Internet, social media, and the almost instantaneous capture and dissemination of visual images in modern times, how has the job of the photojournalist changed?

Anyone with a cell phone can be a photographer now. It’s amazing, but it hasn’t made photography any better. By getting quicker, it’s gotten worse. A hundred photographs a minute, or whatever, does not make necessarily good photography. To me, the digital color war pictures of today are not as compelling as war photographs taken on film, which is interesting because you can go back and look at pictures of Vietnam and WWII, everything before digital, and to me they’re just better. That is only my opinion, and others will certainly disagree.

What do you hope people appreciate when they look at your pictures?

I just hope they like them, that’s all.

This interview is part of a series conducted by Holden Luntz Gallery, based in Palm Beach, Florida.

Interviewer: Sara Tasini

article_text:
Disney+ and Netflix ‘s buying habits appear to be dispelling the notion that non-English-language acquisitions aren’t on their agendas.

Research from Ampere Analysis shows that non-English content now accounts for at least half of acquisitions at both global streamers. As of September, non-English content accounted for 65% of Netflix acquisitions, with the figure at Disney+ hitting 50%.

Japan and Korea were the leading source for Netflix acquisitions, with German and Japanese content topping Disney+’s list.

Related Stories

Cannes Marché & TIFFCOM Commit To Holding Second Edition Of Japan IP Market In 2027

Everything We Know About Netflix's New 'Pride & Prejudice' Series So Far

Ampere noted its research had identified Japanese, French, South Korean and Turkish as the biggest acquisition opportunities moving forwards if high demand and relatively low export volume was considered.

Just 40% of Japanese streaming content is available worldwide, with the U.S. and South Korea the biggest buyers of what can be bought, though France and Germany also show relatively high interest.

Watch on Deadline

It’s a similar story for South Korean content – despite the global popularity of K-drama, only 45% of the country’s titles are available only on its own streaming services. The Middle East and Southeast Asia appear most likely to bite on its romantic-themed films and shows, Ampere claimed.

“Non-English content remains underexploited despite growing global demand. In recent years, Amazon Prime Video, HBO Max and Disney+ have increasingly expanded non-English-language title licensing in multiple markets,” said Tingting Li, Research Manager at Ampere.

“Japanese, South Korean, French and Turkish content present the top opportunities for international licensing, with strong audience appeal but still gaps in cross-border availability. For content owners and platforms, buying this content can bridge the gap between audience demand and international distribution.”

解説・あらすじ

ジョニー・デップが主演を務め、イギリスの文豪チャールズ・ディケンズによる不朽の名作「クリスマス・キャロル」を実写映画化したゴシックファンタジー。 ロンドンに暮らす、強欲で臆病な老人エベネーザ・スクルージ。情に薄く自己中心的でお金しか信用できない彼は、周囲の人々から嫌われていた。クリスマスイブの夜、3人のゴーストが次々とスクルージの前に現れ、それぞれ過去・現在・未来の世界へと連れていく。時空を超えた旅を通して、スクルージはこれまでの自分の人生を見つめ直していく。 孤独なひねくれ者の老人スクルージをデップが怪演し、共演にも「ロード・オブ・ザ・リング」シリーズのイアン・マッケラン、「ハリー・ポッター」シリーズのルパート・グリント、「世界一キライなあなたに」のサム・クラフリン、「スター・ウォーズ」シリーズのデイジー・リドリーら豪華キャストが顔をそろえた。監督は「X エックス」「Pearl パール」「MaXXXine マキシーン」のタイ・ウェスト。

"“我想不会有别人这么做了，”他说。“这绝对是一条艰难得多的路，而且这本来就已经非常困难了。但这是他们的第一直觉，也正是我想要与他们合作的原因。我只知道无论有多难，他们都会做出这些选择，因为它们是正确的，而且他们很感激阻力就是机遇。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": Ringwald）。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在高斯林看来，罗德和米勒为了实现这一点而停下一切的做法，正是这部电影成功的原因所在。“本该是那些带有所有LED的大型视觉场景，结果却只是一把拖把和一副太阳镜，而他们把它放进了电影里。”除了意识到这种自发性有多么重要之外，高斯林还学到了另一件事。“如果你遇到了问题却无法解决，那就去跟朱莉娅·罗伯茨谈谈。这就是这里最大的教训。她会帮你解决的。”", "translated": true}, article_text:
Back in 2020, “ The Martian ” author Andy Weir sent Ryan Gosling a manuscript that hadn’t yet been published, but which he hoped the actor would respond to. When Gosling read “ Project Hail Mary ,” the story of a science teacher tasked with saving the world and stranded in space with only a rock-like alien for company, he felt exactly the way Weir had hoped.

“It felt like this project had a knife in my ribs,” Gosling told me at a Q&A I moderated following a guild screening of the film . “When I put the book down, the knife was saying, ‘OK, now you’re going to call [Phil] Lord and [Chris] Miller, and you’re going to get them to direct this. Then you’re going to get [producer] Amy Pascal to help you, and then you’re going to try to put together the best team there is in the business.’ It just took me hostage.”

Six years later, “ Project Hail Mary ” is one of the biggest critical and commercial hits of 2026 and Gosling is a frontrunner for a well-deserved Oscar nomination. It’s hard to think of many other films of this scale that are so entirely dependent on one actor to do all the heavy lifting. Gosling is in every scene of the 156-minute movie, and he’s called upon to play every note on the tonal scale in a performance that utilizes his razor-sharp comic timing before moving into emotionally devastating registers.

What makes the work all the more impressive is that Gosling has to do all of it without benefit of a scene partner; aside from some flashback scenes depicting his character back on earth, he spends the entire movie with only the alien “Rocky” to act opposite. Luckily, Lord and Miller dismissed the idea of creating Rocky as an entirely computer-generated figure and insisted on having an actor and puppeteer on set to play the alien.

“I don’t think anyone else would have done that,” he said. “It was definitely the much harder route, and this was already very difficult. But it was their first instinct, and it was exactly why I wanted to work with them. I just knew that it didn’t matter how hard it was going to be, they were going make these choices because they were right, and they appreciate that the obstacles are opportunities.”

Those obstacles were plentiful on the set, since the Rocky puppet was often breaking or malfunctioning. “It was like the ‘Jaws’ shark,” he said. “Sometimes just the finger would work.” Rocky was played by James Ortiz, an actor with extensive puppeteering experience who impressed Gosling at his initial audition. There was an immediate rapport, and when Ortiz left the audition Gosling called after him, “Bye, Rocky!”

The problem was that on set it was no longer just Ortiz and Gosling. “It was six puppeteers, dressed like ninjas, and me pretending I couldn’t see them,” he said. Luckily, like Lord and Miller, Ortiz also saw problems and mistakes as opportunities, which Gosling felt mirrored the subject of the film. “We’re all working together to figure out the problem, and it’s what the characters are going through. They’re trying to solve problems so that they can move on with their mission.”

One of Rocky’s most charming attributes, for example, came about because the puppet wasn’t working. “They couldn’t get the arm to turn around to give a thumbs up,” he said. “So we were just like, ‘Let’s go with it,’ and that’s why the puppet gives a thumbs down.” Which isn’t to say that the problem solving was all fun, or Gosling never got tired of the constant challenges.

“I had been acting for a long time on the film, and gone through a lot of incarnations of the character, and really felt like I had tried everything I could think of,” he said. “I had been in a placenta onesie. I looked like a space caveman. I acted like I was born. I acted like I didn’t know how to talk. I was a toddler. I was a man. And by the end of it, we got to this very expensive set, which was all these LED screens we had been waiting for to be built. We invested a lot of money in that, and it was very visually beautiful and fancy and high-tech. But I was just so tired of acting alone.”

Gosling went outside for some air, and saw Julia Roberts. “I’d never met her, and she sat down and talked to me,” he said. “She was talking about how much fun she was having on her set with Luca Guadagnino on ‘After the Hunt.’ She said, ‘You should come over,’ and I needed human interaction. So I went down to the set, and they were shooting a party scene, and they were all drinking and having fun, and they seemed like they were having a great time.”

When Gosling returned to the “Project Hail Mary” set, he told Lord and Miller he was tired of acting alone. “I said, ‘I want a friend, I want someone to act with,'” he said. “They were like, ‘OK, but what do we do?’ And I said, ‘I want to get a mop, and I want to make it into a person and talk to it.’ And they stopped everything on our fancy, expensive day, and crawled around the sets looking for tape and glasses, and a dress. And they helped me build this mop lady for me to do scenes with, who we called Moppy Ringwald.”

As Gosling sees it, the fact that Lord and Miller stopped everything to make that happen is emblematic of why the film worked. “What were supposed to be these great visual scenes with all these LEDs, it was just a mop and sunglasses, and they put it in the movie.” In addition to realizing how important that kind of spontaneity could be, Gosling learned something else as well. “If you’re having a problem and you can’t solve it, talk to Julia Roberts. That’s the big lesson here. She’ll solve it for you.”

“Project Hail Mary” is currently streaming on Prime Video.

article_text:
‘Water: Our Shared Story’ invites photographers worldwide to document how water shapes our world and the people who depend on it with a US$23,000 prize pool

HIPA has launched ‘Water: Our Shared Story’, a global photography competition inviting photographers to explore one of the world’s most vital resources through compelling visual storytelling.

Held in cooperation with the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the 2026 United Nations Water Conference, the competition comes ahead of the UN conference, which will take place in Abu Dhabi from 8-10 December 2026. Photographers worldwide are invited to submit a photo story of 5-10 photographs with a total prize pool of US$23,000.

Commenting on the competition, Ali Bin Thalith, Secretary General of HIPA, said: “We are proud to collaborate with the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the 2026 UN Water Conference by using the cultural and awareness-raising power of photography to encourage a global conversation about water. We invite photographers and photography communities worldwide to participate and share visual stories that are compelling, accessible and impactful, supporting the objectives of the conference.”

Entries close on 15 October 2026. Full competition rules, eligibility requirements and submission details are available on the official HIPA website: www.hipa.ae .

{"type": "paragraph", "text": "「週末はかなり騒然とした状況でしたが、フェアの開幕直後から、アートに対する確かな熱気を感じています。パリには独特の魅力があります。矛盾を抱え、絶えず変化するエネルギーに満ち、至るところで驚きを与えてくれる街です。パリの標語である『Fluctuat nec "「私たちにとって重要なのは、自分たち自身がワクワクし続けることだけでなく、ほかの人々にも刺激を与え、新たな問いを投げかけることです」とライアーは語る。「今は、自分たちがどのように活動し、何をどう提示し、どのように協力関係を築くのかについて、非常に柔軟な姿勢を持つ必要があります」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "「今日のコレクターは、以前ほど価格を信用しておらず、提示された価格をそのまま受け入れることもありません」とナハブは語り、こう続ける。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": アート・バーゼル・パリ2026が開幕。メガギャラリーの売れ行きは好調、共同ブースは過去最多に

フランス各地で抗議活動が続くなか、 アート・バーゼル・パリ 2026の招待制プレビュー「アヴァン・プルミエール」が10月20日に開催された。主要ギャラリーが高額作品の売却を報告したほか、共同ブースも過去最多の12カ所に上り、市場の調整期におけるギャラリー間の協働も広がりを見せた。

週末に行われた抗議デモの痕跡が街の至るところに残るパリだが、アート界は変わらず動いていた。10月19日と20日には展覧会のオープニングや関連イベントが開かれ、20日午後3時には アート・バーゼル・パリ のアヴァン・プルミエールが幕を開けた。

2025年に新設されたアヴァン・プルミエールは、通常のVIPプレビューに先立って行われる招待制の内覧会だ。今年は開場10分前になっても大きな行列ができず、前年よりやや落ち着いた雰囲気だった。会場内は一部の通路で混雑が見られたものの、比較的スムーズに移動でき、大手ギャラリーのブースには購入意欲の高いコレクターが集まっていた。これは、フェアや各ギャラリーが招待客を慎重に選び、購買につながるコレクターに絞り込んだ結果なのかもしれない。

抗議活動が続くも、有力コレクターが来場

一部のディーラーやアート・アドバイザーによれば、抗議活動を懸念して渡仏を取りやめたコレクターもいたと語った。アメリカのコレクターは姿を見せないのではないかという懸念もあったが、会場では「 TOP 200 COLLECTORS 」に名を連ねる アリソン・バーグ や グレン・ファーマン 、 パメラ・ジョイナー らの姿が見られた。また、俳優のケイティ・ホームズやナタリー・ポートマンに加え、 ロサンゼルス・カウンティ美術館 のCEOを務めるマイケル・ゴヴァンや MoMA PS1のキュレーター、 ルバ・カトリブ など、アメリカの美術機関関係者も来場していた。

アート・アドバイザーのアナ・ソロコフはUS版ARTnewsの取材に対し、会場内の展示について「キュレーションが巧みで、細部までよく考えられています」と評価した。さらに、会場となったグラン・パレの魅力にも触れ、「ここは魔法のような場所です」とコメントしている。

ディーラーたちは今年のアヴァン・プルミエールについて、「活気がある」と口をそろえた。パリを拠点とするタンプロンのマチュー・タンプロンも、開始から1時間あまりが経った時点で「地元での開催ということもあり、幸先のいいスタートを切れています」と語った。同ギャラリーは、ビラル・ハムダッドの《L’envers du soir》（2026）を6万5000ユーロ（約1150万円）で販売したと報告している。ハムダッドは昨年、アート・バーゼル・パリの会期中にプティ・パレで個展を開いており、タンプロンによれば、作品への引き合いは引き続き強く、来年3月に予定されている個展にも高い関心が寄せられているという。

アヴァン・プルミエールは開催時間が限られるため、ほとんどのギャラリーの販売報告は1〜2件にとどまった。初日から多数の売約が報告される他都市の アート・バーゼル や、今月18日に終了した フリーズ・ロンドン とは対照的だ。

ロンドンとパリのアートシーンは、これまでもたびたび比較されてきた。ニューヨークとサンパウロを拠点とするコレクターのウィル・ペーリーは、 フリーズ とアート・バーゼルを「補完的な関係」と捉え、その違いを次のように説明した。

「フリーズは主に新進ギャラリーや若手アーティスト、より挑戦的な作品を求める若いコレクターに向けたフェアです。一方、アート・バーゼル・パリでは、より高額な作品が扱われています」

メガギャラリーの売れ行きは好調

ハウザー＆ワース のプレジデント、マーク・ペイヨも、有力コレクターが集まることをこのフェアの強みと捉えている。しかし同時に、「難しいのは、街そのものにも魅力があることです。来場者はフェアだけを見るためにパリを訪れるわけではありません」と指摘する。フェアは、彼らの訪問目的のひとつにすぎないのだ。

タデウス・ロパック も、パリにはフェア以外に来場者の関心を引くものが多いと指摘する。そのためか、「パリではコレクターが購入を決めるのが早い」と感じているという。21日朝のVIPプレビューに再び訪れると話す顧客がいる一方、美術館やギャラリーの展覧会を優先したり、ショッピングを楽しんだりするために、アヴァン・プルミエールへの参加を見送る顧客もいた。それでもロパックをはじめとするディーラーたちは、かつてはスイスのアート・バーゼルでしか見られなかったような希少で高額な作品も、積極的にパリに出品している。

ロパックによれば、1906年から1938年にかけて制作された パブロ・ピカソ の作品4点のほか、 ルーチョ・フォンタナ の1953年のミクストメディア作品が180万ユーロ（約3億2000万円）、 ゲオルク・バゼリッツ の2019年の作品が80万ユーロ（約1億4200万円）で売却されたという。「非常に好調です。正直なところ、期待を大きく上回るわけではありませんが」とロパックは語る。

ペイヨは、通常のギャラリーでの取引に比べ、アートフェアでは売買が早く成立する傾向があると説明する。それでも、コレクターは購入を決めるまでに時間をかけるようになったという。

「約5年前と比べると、間違いなくペースは遅くなっています。それでも、優れた作品は最終的にふさわしいコレクションに収まるものです」

こうしたなか、ハウザー＆ワースは20日午後の短時間で、 ゲルハルト・リヒター の《Rokokotisch (Rococo Table)》（1965）を1000万ドル台（約15億8200万円以上）で売却している。この希少な初期作品は、事前のプレビューには含まれておらず、ブースに急きょ追加されたものだった。

また、ゲオルク・バゼリッツの《Der Hirte》（1965）には1000万ドル台で買い手が付いている。さらに、 ジョージ・コンド の《Woman with Designer Shirt》（2026）を290万ドル（約4億6000万円）、ルーチョ・フォンタナの《Concetto spaziale》（1961）を170万ユーロ（約3億円）、 フィリップ・ガストン の《Untitled》（1969）を150万ドル（約2億3700万円）、 アレクサンダー・カルダー の《Four Dots and Brass Tail》（1953年頃）を100万ドル弱（約1億5800万円）で売却した。

1億ドル超のモディリアーニ作品も登場

ペース、ディ・ドンナ・ギャラリーズ、デイヴィッド・シュレーダーが2025年に共同設立したペース・ディ・ドンナ・シュレーダー（PDS）は、今回のフェアで最も高額とみられる作品を出品した。 アメデオ・モディリアーニ が横たわる裸婦を描いた油彩画《Nu étendu (Lolotte)》（1917）で、提示価格は1億ドル（約158億円）を超える。同ギャラリーによると、この作品が一般公開されるのは約1世紀ぶりだという。1917年にギャラリー・ベルト・ヴェイユで開かれたモディリアーニの生涯唯一の個展にも出品されており、同展は裸婦画がわいせつとみなされたことで物議を醸した。

PDSの共同創設者であるエマニュエル・ディ・ドンナは、フェアの滑り出しは「引き合いが殺到し、対応が追いつかない」ほど非常に好調だったと語る。ただし、モディリアーニの作品は買い手が決まるまでに時間がかかると見ている。

ガゴシアン は具体的な販売価格を明かさなかったものの、1987年制作の ウィレム・デ・クーニング 作品を1000万ドル以上（約15億8160万円以上）で販売したほか、 ピーター・ドイグ の作品も買い手がついたと発表した。 ホワイト・キューブ は、 ジュリー・メレツ による2001年と2018年制作の絵画2点がそれぞれ785万ドル（約12億4150万円）で売れたほか、計16点の販売を報告。また、ピカソ作品が15万ユーロ（約2660万円）、 フェルナン・レジェ 作品が6万5000ユーロ（約1150万円）で売れるなど、歴史的な作家による紙作品も好調だったという。

このほか、US版ARTnewsが確認した販売実績には、 グラッドストーン が出品したヴィクター・マンの絵画が30万ドル（約4700万円）、ワンゲチ・ムトゥのコラージュ作品2点がそれぞれ32万5000ドル（約5140万円）、クリマンツットが11万ドル（約1740万円）で販売したヤン・ヘギュの彫刻作品などが売れた。

ブリュッセルを拠点とするギャラリスト、ザビエル・ハフケンスは10点の販売を報告し、最高額はシャーリン・フォン・ハイルの絵画で47万5000ドル（約7510万円）だった。ハフケンスはメールで次のようにコメントしている。

「週末はかなり騒然とした状況でしたが、フェアの開幕直後から、アートに対する確かな熱気を感じています。パリには独特の魅力があります。矛盾を抱え、絶えず変化するエネルギーに満ち、至るところで驚きを与えてくれる街です。パリの標語である『Fluctuat nec mergitur（たゆたえども沈まず）』は、まさに今週の状況にふさわしい言葉だと感じます」

過去最多の共同ブースが示す市場の変化

デイヴィッド・コルダンスキーのパートナー、マイク・ホーマーは、購入を検討していた複数の作品が実際の成約に至ったと語る。「作品を実際に目にし、あらゆる角度から鑑賞したいという欲求があることを裏付けています。これは喜ばしい回帰です」

同ギャラリーで成約した作品の一つが、サム・ギリアムによる希少なハードエッジ抽象絵画《Mycenaean Ode》（1965）で、販売価格は30万ドル。

今年のフェアでは、24のギャラリーが参加する共同ブースが過去最多となる12カ所設けられた。その好例が、会場2階に設置された、ウィーンのライアーとベルリンおよびミュンヘンを拠点とするクラウパ＝トゥスカニー・ツァイドラーの共同ブースだ。両ギャラリーとも複数の作品を販売したという。

アマデオ・クラウパ＝トゥスカニーは、「著名なコレクションに収蔵してもらいたいと考えていた作品を数多く販売できたので、とても満足しています」と語り、販売先はいずれもヨーロッパのコレクションだったと明かした。一方、エマニュエル・ライアーは、アメリカのコレクターにも作品を販売したと付け加えた。

共同ブースでは、両ギャラリーが扱う歴史的作品と現代作品を組み合わせて展示していた。その一つが、奇妙な形の松葉杖のように使用することで、人の動き方を変化させるフランツ・ヴェストの彫刻作品《Passstück》（1983／1984）だ。その隣には、アンナ・ウッデンベルグの《White Noise (Soft Skills)》（2026）が展示されていた。オフィス用の人間工学に基づいた家具や器具を未来的に再解釈した構造物によって、顔のない等身大のマネキンの身体がねじ曲げられた彫刻作品だ。

「私たちにとって重要なのは、自分たち自身がワクワクし続けることだけでなく、ほかの人々にも刺激を与え、新たな問いを投げかけることです」とライアーは語る。「今は、自分たちがどのように活動し、何をどう提示し、どのように協力関係を築くのかについて、非常に柔軟な姿勢を持つ必要があります」

アートアドバイザリー会社、NGパートナーズの共同創業者であるニコラ・ナハブも、アート市場が引き続き「調整期」にある中、ギャラリーが協働のための創造的な方法を模索する動きが広がっていると指摘する。その背景には、特にウルトラ・コンテンポラリー作品の価格に対する懐疑的な見方があるという。

「今日のコレクターは、以前ほど価格を信用しておらず、提示された価格をそのまま受け入れることもありません」とナハブは語り、こう続ける。

「こうした信頼の欠如によって、コレクターは提供された情報に疑問を抱き、吟味するようになっています。購入を決断する前に、安心できるだけの裏付けや調査、そして作家の制作活動と市場における位置づけについての包括的な理解を求めています。意思決定にこれほど時間がかかるのは、そのためです。翻って言えば、信頼関係さえ築かれていれば、コレクターにとって決断は容易なのです」

（翻訳：編集部）

article_text:
Photographer Harley Weir and fashion designer Dilara Findikoglu have joined forces for Witch , a photo book published by IDEA , bringing together powerful women and real witches to explore the relationship between femininity, nature, spirituality and rebellion. It asks: What does the word ‘Witch’ mean today?

Rooted in Romania’s traditions of folk magic and mythology, the book challenges the historical misinterpretation of witchcraft. The witch became a figure of fear, embodying everything that patriarchal society sought to control. Similarly, women who challenged social expectations or refused to conform have been marginalised and persecuted. Witch reclaims this vilified narrative as a symbol of defiance and knowledge; it celebrates women who embrace their identities and feminine power.

Travelling across eight cities and villages over five days, Weir and Findikoglu are in discussion with a diverse spectrum of women. Delving into the limitless power of being a woman and the importance of regaining our spirituality and sacred connection with nature. The natural power and energy all women possess inside of themselves, just waiting to be invoked.

“We photographed real witches, and powerful women on a journey across Romania. For centuries, the witch has been used as a symbol of evil. But maybe she was never scary because she was evil, maybe she was scary because she was free. Across history, women who were outspoken, independent, sexual, knowledgeable, or simply unwilling to conform have been treated as dangerous. The witch became a name for the woman who could not, or would not, be controlled.

“Dilara Findikoglu’s clothes become part of this story. Her designs embrace femininity without making it obedient. The body as a place of rebellion, desire and self-expression. The clothes feel protective and provocative at once, allowing these women to inhabit the witch not as a caricature of evil, but as a symbol of power, freedom and refusal.

“Among the women we photographed were Mihaela Minca and her daughters. Known locally and worldwide as the most powerful witches alive. In them, the witch is not a myth but a lived reality, a way of being rooted in nature, tradition, and feminine knowledge outside institutional power.

“This zine is a celebration of women, the complicated, the powerful, the unruly, the tender, the strange and the unapologetic. Women. Witches.” – Harley Weir

“The word witch has long been used to marginalise a form of power and wisdom associated with women. By linking the feminine relationship with nature and the unseen, society transformed what it could not understand into something to fear.

“For centuries, patriarchal thinking has placed logic, reason and control above intuition, emotion and instinct. Yet these are equally valuable forms of knowledge, each essential to our understanding of existence. The wisdom associated with the feminine is not something mystical or extraordinary, but something deeply rooted in our bodies, our connection to nature and the knowledge we carry within us.

“Through this book, we wanted to explore and celebrate the beauty of this often overlooked wisdom. To question the boundaries between the rational and the unseen, and to recognise the power that exists beyond what we have been taught to understand as truth.

“Having Eastern European roots myself, travelling through Romania and meeting the women there felt strangely familiar. There was something beautiful about the land and its people, and a sense that the ancient knowledge and traditions we had come to explore were still very much alive.” – Dilara Findikoglu

Harley’s visceral direction paired with Dilara’s evocative garments through the lens of the modern woman in her spiritual landscape. Embodying tradition, legacy and our somewhat lost divine connection with nature.

An entrancing marriage between traditional dress and couture, this series of photographs and interviews tells a generational story of the evolution of witchcraft and womanhood today. Redefining a draconian history composed by the male perspective.

article_text:
The Afterlife of Flowers

The cemetery is not merely a place of absence, but a silent theatre in which nature performs its most extreme and poetic act. Among the vases of various shapes – whether abandoned or tended – an unintentional art form unfolds: still lifes born of chance, shaped by the wind, lashed by the rain and baked by the sun. In this portfolio, the dried flowers are not mere remnants, but narrative voices. Each one embodies a state of the soul: at times abandonment, at times solitude, at times the very moment of passing. Their structural and chromatic transformations become the metronome of passing time, a vegetal hourglass in which every petal that curls or crumbles marks the slow fading of memory. A fragile beauty hovers around these compositions, veiled by a subtle melancholy. Under the blinding light of day, these floral remnants stand stubbornly firm, laden with feelings that refuse to fade, suspended in the eternal moment that precedes their final transformation into dust and earth.

carmelomicieli.altervista.org

“THE AFTERLIFE OF FLOWERS” (L’aldilà dei fiori) Il cimitero non è soltanto il luogo dell’assenza, ma un teatro silenzioso in cui la natura compie il suo atto più estremo e poetico. Tra i vasi di forme diverse, abbandonati o curati, si consuma una forma d’arte involontaria: nature morte nate dal caso, modellate dal vento, sferzate dalla pioggia e cotte dal sole. In questo portfolio, i fiori secchi non sono semplici residui, ma voci narranti. Ciascuno di essi custodisce una condizione dell’anima: ora l’abbandono, ora la solitudine, ora il momento esatto del trapasso. Le loro mutazioni strutturali e cromatiche diventano il metronomo del tempo che passa, una clessidra vegetale in cui ogni petalo che si incurva o si sfarina segna il lento consumarsi della memoria. Intorno a queste composizioni aleggia una bellezza fragile, velata da una malinconia sottile. Sotto la luce accecante del giorno, questi resti floreali resistono testardi, carichi di sentimenti che non vogliono svanire, sospesi nell’attimo eterno che precede la loro definitiva trasformazione in polvere e terra.

article_text:
Joseph Mazzello , the “Bohemian Rhapsody” and “Jurassic Park” actor, heads the cast of “ A Grim Life ,” a supernatural thriller set inside Los Angeles’ Cecil Hotel.

Hong Kong outfit Cappu Films has picked up international sales, it was unveiled at the Tokyo International Film Festival ‘s TIFFCOM market.

Francesco Lucente writes and directs. Mazzello, whose credits also take in “The Pacific,” plays Tom, a filmmaker down on his luck who pays the bills scrubbing toilets and can’t stop reworking the one script he has. A friend steers him toward “Böse,” a lost silent picture from 1931, and Tom’s hunt for an artistic breakthrough pulls him toward a dark secret.

Related Stories

'The Big Boom!,' Documentary About Weapons Factory Workers, Picked Up by Lightdox Ahead of IDFA Premiere (EXCLUSIVE)

'Women and War,' About Ukrainian Women Undergoing Trauma Therapy, Acquired by Rise and Shine World Sales (EXCLUSIVE)

Max Beesley (“Jack Ryan”) plays producer Joe, with Wes Studi (“Avatar: Fire and Ash”) as Nic, Carl Lumbly (“Captain America: Brave New World”) as Henry and Arnetia Walker (“Bookie”) as Chelsea. Studi is a 2019 recipient of an Academy Honorary Award.

The building itself does much of the work. The film draws its scares from the hotel’s hallways and concealed rooms, leaning on sound, shadow and Tom’s deepening isolation to tighten the dread.

Lucente also produces. The project will move into pre-production in December 2026 ahead of a January 2027 shoot, with delivery penciled for July 2027.

“‘A Grim Life’ is a deeply personal project for me, one that explores the darker side of ambition, obsession, and the sacrifices we make in pursuit of our dreams,” Lucente said. “The Cecil Hotel provides an extraordinary and haunting backdrop for a story where the boundaries between reality and the supernatural begin to disappear.”

Cappu first presented the film to buyers in Busan and is keeping those conversations going before cameras roll. Janice Woo of Cappu Films said the Cecil Hotel and the lost film give the project an immediately compelling premise, “while Tom’s desperation gives the story its emotional center.” She added: “Following our work with Francesco on ‘Starbright,’ we’re pleased to continue the relationship with a project that brings together a distinctive atmosphere and an experienced cast.”

Lucente previously directed the drama “Badland” and the fantasy “Starbright,” which stars Ted Levine, John Rhys-Davies and Diego Boneta.

Besides “Starbright,” the Cappu slate carries another Lucente fantasy, “Sinbad,” plus the action titles “Lion Fist” and “Red Bird.” The company’s catalog spans horror, fantasy, action and arthouse fare, and also includes TV series and library titles from Hong Kong cinema’s Golden Era.

title_original: Everything That Dies Someday Comes Back: Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere
editorial_title_zh: 终将逝去的一切终会复萌：《斯普林斯汀：从无到有》
editorial_excerpt_zh: 没有“老板”的Boss：斯科特·库珀的《斯普林斯汀：从无到有》未能找到一种真诚的方式来展现创作音乐的日常过程
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我想往这些荒地（Badlands）的脸上吐口水，”布鲁斯·斯普林斯汀（Bruce Springsteen）于1980年11月在亚利桑那州的一个舞台上咆哮道，他吐出的字句仿佛卡在心头一般。这场演出恰好在罗纳德·里根（Ronald Reagan）压倒性赢得总统大选的第二天举行，是布鲁斯为其双专辑《The River》展开的历时一年、令人精疲力竭的巡演中的早期一站。在那段时期里，他与E街乐队（E Street Band）的马拉松式演唱会开始接近古典歌剧的体量，演出时长直逼4小时，歌单则膨胀到近40首歌。在这些摇滚乐咏叹调不断延伸的空间里，布鲁斯将“Rosalita”和“Tenth Avenue Freeze-Out”等早期职业生涯的热门金曲演绎得狂喜激昂，但他也将那些赤裸、无情的歌曲打造成体育场级别的摇滚奇观，这些歌曲揭露了美国梦核心处已经腐烂的本质。那天夜里在坦佩，一段哀怨的口琴声给赋予了专辑（及巡演）名称的歌曲《The River》留下了创伤；不祥的管风琴低鸣和小军鼓的重击推动着《Factory》这首歌，它是献给他的父亲道格拉斯·“荷兰人”·斯普林斯汀（Douglas “Dutch” Springsteen）的，据这位歌手吐露，父亲一生从未得到过除此之外的任何东西——“工作、劳作，唯有劳作的人生”。正如其歌词所宣告的那样，充满激昂愿景、描绘“腹地困境”（trouble in the heartland）的《Badlands》同样也是这些较黑暗的歌曲之一。在亚利桑那州的舞台上，他以如此增压的愤怒演绎着这首歌，感觉就像是在往里根的眼睛里吐口水一样。", "links": [{"text": "snarls", "url": "https://filmcomment.us8.list-manage.com/track/click?u=bea725f8e0ef56b82be4ae760&id=4b1dd38525&e=270138fa20"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "相似的一幕展现了布鲁斯火力全开的“老板”姿态，它拉开了斯科特·库珀（Scott Cooper）新片《斯普林斯汀：从虚无中拯救我》（Springstein: Deliver Me from Nowhere）的序幕，该片是今年纽约电影节的聚光灯晚会精选影片。故事始于“母亲河”巡演，但时间定格在81年9月辛辛那提的闭幕演出上，杰瑞米·艾伦·怀特（Jeremy Allen White）取代了布鲁斯。虽然不可否认存在一种奇妙的身体违和感（本质上看起来就像知名演员杰瑞米·艾伦·怀特突然跳上舞台，开始随机模仿布鲁斯·斯普林斯汀，而且模仿得还算不错），但他确实拿捏住了布鲁斯那种孔雀开屏般的特质——扭头、捏下巴、把头仰向天空，以及那宽得刚好透出几分大步流星之感的站姿。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，事情有些不对劲的第一个线索与其说在于该场景拥有什么，不如说在于它遗漏了什么。如果说亚利桑那州的布鲁斯在演唱《Badlands》时看起来几乎像个宗教狂热分子，沉浸在与乐队成员的强力互动中，并被歌曲本身净化力量的信念所支配，那么《斯普林斯汀：从无到有》中辛辛那提的布鲁斯则在一首几乎无可挑剔、相当不错的《Born to Run》中一路卖弄风骚，而这首歌到1981年时已经问世6年了。库珀与摄影指导（DP）高坂昌义（Masanobu Takayanagi）的镜头似乎无法信任他们所选择的表演者的个人魅力，在观众席中欢呼挥手的、油滑而崇拜的人海与舞台上日益汗流浃背、情绪高涨的怀特之间进行了反复而陈旧的交叉剪辑——这显然是企图给其饱经劳累的面部轮廓镀上一层明星般的光泽。随着歌曲冲向其可以预见的结局——全场观众为之狂热崇拜；接着猛然剪辑到后台孤身一人、疲惫不堪、双手抱头的布鲁斯——我们开始感觉到某种叙事正被强加给我们，一个关于聚光灯下生活的沉浮、再熟悉不过的故事。但代价是什么呢？舞台上那个亚利桑那州的家伙又当如何？他似乎能如此娴熟、如此无可否认地挥洒着他的政治怒火与音乐承诺。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "摇滚传记片——尤其是近期涌现的一批聚焦于弗雷迪·墨丘利（Bryan Singer和Dexter Fletcher执导的《波西米亚狂想曲》）、鲍勃·迪伦（詹姆斯·曼高德执导的《完全未知》）以及埃尔维斯（巴兹·鲁赫曼执导的……呃……《猫王》）等偶像的电影——总是围绕着模仿而构建。现在，它轮到了“老板”。在这些电影中，演员的拟仿能力只能发挥到一定程度，随后便会与他们所崇拜的名人那至今历久弥新的声音与影像发生碰撞。当我们观看时，它似乎总是把我们置于一种不断变幻、有时充满评判、有时又怪异的位置。尽管我们做出了最高尚的努力去暂停怀疑，但我们还是被卷入了一场评估的游戏，像《美国偶像》（American Idol）的评委一样，给这个或那个模仿的信服度打分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为这场纷争中的最新两部作品，《斯普林斯汀》和《迪伦》电影由于其主角目前依然健在而变得加倍复杂——这些并不是那种可以通过奥斯汀·巴特勒（Austin Butler）和拉米·马雷克（Rami Malek）试图复活带有鬓角的传奇猫王和留着小胡子的墨丘利那样的方式来“起死回生”的角色。相反，这两部电影都以更加低调的姿态呈现自己，它们就像是那种专注于关系的室友剧和世纪中期年代剧——或许可以以罗伯特·雷德福（Robert Redford）的《大河恋》（1992）和南希·萨沃卡（Nancy Savoca）的《狗斗》（1991）等作品为代表——这些曾是主流及独立美国电影的中流砥柱。影片在具有历史唤起力的美术设计上倾注了极大心血，每部叙事的核心利害关系则围绕着如何通过为我们这位天才却又神秘的主角安排一个极其人性化且脚踏实地的浪漫对象，来让他的形象变得复杂立体。但尽管这两部电影愿意把自己标榜为匠心独运的怀旧之作，人们也不可避免地会把它们放在当下大肆 churning 的IP工厂（涵盖特许经营、重启和电影宇宙）的当代背景下去审视，在那里，微型衍生剧和“起源故事”为未来继续靠相同产品捞金留下了充足空间。斯普林斯汀和迪伦最近分别以数亿美元的价格将他们全部作品的版权出售给了庞大的媒体巨头——索尼（Sony）和环球（Universal），这或许并非巧合。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不过，库珀选择采用与《完全未知》（A Complete Unknown）相似的框架，将视野缩小到其传记对象生活和职业生涯的一个特定转折点，这仍然不失为一种明智的选择。在去年的这部传记片中，聚焦的是迪伦早年在格林尼治村的日子，直到1965年的纽波特民谣节——正是在那里，他上演了著名的“插电”事件。而在本片中，则是关于专辑《内布拉斯加》（Nebraska）的创作。这张斯普林斯汀于1982年创作的如幽灵般的杰作，当年是在新泽西州科尔茨内克一间铺着长毛地毯的卧室里，用一台挑剔的四轨盒式录音机录制的。在电影的叙述中，布鲁斯拖着被掏空的身体结束了“母亲河”巡演，随即陷入了一种虽沮丧却富有成效的离群索居之中。他偶尔走出水库旁租来的房子，或是若有所思地凝视附近破败的童年故居，或是在他曾经的老据点“斯通波尼”（The Stone Pony）酒吧与一支硬摇滚蓝调乐队纵情弹奏吉他Solo。在那里，他遇到了费伊（奥黛莎·杨饰），一个高中某个家伙的妹妹，两人展开了一段温柔却日渐充满情感张力的恋情。深夜偶然在电视上看到泰伦斯·马利克（Terence Malick）的《恶土》（1973）激发了他的创作灵感，让他文思泉涌，从“Born in the USA”和“I'm on Fire”这样稳操胜券的热门歌曲，到那些荒凉、简朴的连环杀手、高速公路巡警以及深夜驾驶员的故事，最终都汇集到了《内布拉斯加》这张专辑中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与此同时，斯蒂芬·格雷厄姆（Stephen Graham）和加比·霍夫曼（Gaby Hoffmann）在片中的黑白闪回片段里频频现身，宛如他的父母一般如影随形；而大肆抢戏的杰瑞米·强劲（Jeremy Strong）则饰演布鲁斯的经纪人乔恩·兰道（Jon Landau），他身着全套80年代运动服饰，在片中来回穿梭。一个颇具启示意义的选择是，兰道这位颇有建树的制作人和评论家，在片中被塑造成了一种介于炒作推手和生活教练之间的人物，其主要作用是将布鲁斯的艺术转化为面向哥伦比亚广播公司（CBS）西服革履高管们的企业黑话：“在这个办公室，我的办公室里，我们信仰布鲁斯·斯普林斯汀。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《从虚无中拯救我》对剖析身为表演者的斯普林斯汀兴致索然，而对于身为词曲创作者的他则更是缺乏兴趣。对于一部核心剧情主要围绕一张专辑的创作与录制展开的电影而言，它却找不到一种真诚的方式去想象歌词创作和音乐制作的日常过程。相反，身兼编剧的库珀只能生搬硬套一些关于生活与艺术的笨拙且虚假的等同关系。片中有一幕，布鲁斯在研究查尔斯·斯塔克韦瑟——那个启发了马利克《恶土》的现实生活中的杀手——时，疯狂地涂写着“为什么？”，这让我想起了杰森·伯恩（Jason Bourne）那些笨拙的尝试：通过在笔记本上填满半记不清的词句、涂鸦以及诸如“我是谁？”之类的问题来揭开自己的过去。在最糟糕的情况下，这部电影完全依仗于一种虚假的直白联系：将布鲁斯那些日益黑暗复杂的歌曲与他源自童年创伤的抑郁划上等号，这一切都通过前面提到的闪回片段暗示出来——仿佛艺术表达的意义和效力可以完全用其创作者的精神健康来解释清楚，具体到本片中，就是被简单归结为布鲁斯与父亲的关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "将这些歌曲仅仅框定为“布鲁斯正在经历的事情”，也让影片得以就音乐的商业可行性（或缺乏可行性）渲染出人为的戏剧冲突，强尼·强（Jeremy Strong）饰演的兰道在布鲁斯的忧郁与唱片高管、录音师组成的“现实世界”之间充当润滑剂。因此，片中展现布鲁斯与E街乐队在录音室录制“Born in the article_text:
“I wanna spit in the face of these Badlands,” Bruce Springsteen snarls from an Arizona stage in November 1980, hurling out the words as if they’d been stuck in his guts. The show, held just one day after Ronald Reagan’s landslide presidential-election victory, was an early stop on Bruce’s grueling yearlong tour for his double album The River —an era in which his marathon concerts with the E Street Band began to approach the scope of classical operas, with runtimes pushing past four hours and set lists ballooning toward 40 songs. In the expanding space of these rock ’n’ roll arias, Bruce worked ecstatic rave-ups out of early-career hits like “Rosalita” and “Tenth Avenue Freeze-Out,” but he also crafted stadium-rock spectacles out of stark, unrelenting songs that exposed a rotten core at the center of the American Dream. That night in Tempe, a plaintive harmonica leaves its scars on the song that gave the album (and the tour) its name, “The River”; an ominous organ drone and snare-drum thump drives “Factory,” a song dedicated to his father, Douglas “Dutch” Springsteen, who, the singer confides, was never afforded anything beyond “the work, the working, just the working life.” A pumped-up vision, as its lyrics pronounce, of “trouble in the heartland,” “Badlands” was one of these darker songs, too. On stage in Arizona, he performs it with such turbocharged rage that it feels like he’s spitting right in Reagan’s eyes.

A similar scene depicting Bruce going full Boss Mode kicks off Scott Cooper’s new movie Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere , the Spotlight Gala selection of this year’s New York Film Festival. We begin on the River Tour, but with its closing show in Cincinnati, in September ’81, and Jeremy Allen White has been swapped in for Bruce. While there’s an admittedly strange physical disconnect (it essentially just looks like noted actor Jeremy Allen White hopped on stage and randomly started doing a pretty good Bruce Springsteen impersonation), he really does nail that very Bruce kind of peacocking—the craning and pinching of the chin, the head tilting skyward, the stance just wide enough to suggest that particular broad-legged strut.

But the first clue that something’s not quite right lies not so much in what the scene has going for it as in what it leaves out. Where the Arizona Bruce of “Badlands” appears almost like a religious fanatic, channeling the electric interplay with his bandmates and possessed by belief in the cleansing power of the song itself, the Cincinnati Bruce of Deliver Me from Nowhere mugs his way through a note-perfect, pretty-much-fine version of “Born to Run,” a song that by 1981 was already six years old. Cooper and DP Masanobu Takayanagi’s camera can’t seem to trust in the charisma of their chosen performer, repeatedly and stalely crosscutting between a glibly adoring sea of waving hands in the audience and an increasingly sweaty and animated White on stage—an apparent attempt at bestowing a starlike sheen on the laboring contours of his face. As the song hurtles to its predictable conclusion—the crowd going wild in adulation; a smash cut to a wearied Bruce alone backstage, head in hands—we start to sense that a certain kind of narrative is being foisted on us, an all-too-familiar one about the highs and lows of life in the limelight. But at what cost? What about that guy on stage in Arizona, who seemed to wield his political fury and musical commitment so deftly, so undeniably?

The rock biopic, particularly a recent slew devoted to icons like Freddie Mercury (Bryan Singer and Dexter Fletcher’s Bohemian Rhapsody ), Bob Dylan (James Mangold’s A Complete Unknown ), and Elvis (Baz Luhrmann’s… umm… Elvis ), is always built around an imitation. Now it comes for the Boss. In these films, the mimetic powers of an actor can go only so far before bumping up against the still-enduring sounds and images of their celebrity muse. As we watch, it constantly seems to put us in a shifting, sometimes judgmental, sometimes uncanny position. Despite our noblest efforts at suspending disbelief, we get sucked into a game of assessment, ranking the convincingness of this or that impersonation as if we were judges on American Idol.

As the two latest entries into the fray, the Springsteen and Dylan films are doubly complicated by the fact that their subjects are still very much here with us—these aren’t characters who can be “brought back to life” in the way that Austin Butler and Rami Malek attempt to resurrect the mythic Elvis with his sideburns and Mercury with his mustache. Instead, both films present themselves on much more modest terms, as the kind of relationship-focused chamber dramas and mid-century period pieces—perhaps typified by works like Robert Redford’s A River Runs Through It (1992) and Nancy Savoca’s Dogfight (1991)—that used to be a staple of mainstream and independent American cinema. Great care is lavished on historically evocative production design, and the essential stakes of each narrative revolves around making our genius but enigmatic main man somehow complicated by setting him up with an all-too-human and grounded love interest. But as much as these two films would like to think of themselves as craftsmanlike throwbacks, they’re also impossible not to view in the contemporary context of the ever-churning IP mill of franchises, reboots, and cinematic universes, where bite-size spin-offs and “origin stories” leave ample room for future chances to cash in on the same products. It’s perhaps not a coincidence that both Springsteen and Dylan recently sold the publishing rights to their entire catalogues to megalith media corporations—Sony and Universal, respectively—for multi–hundred million dollar price tags.

Still, there’s some wisdom in Cooper’s choice to adopt a similar frame to A Complete Unknown , narrowing the parameters to a specific inflection point in his subject’s life and career. In last year’s biopic, it was Dylan’s early years in Greenwich Village up to the 1965 Newport Folk Festival, where he famously “went electric.” Here, it’s the making of the Nebraska album, Springsteen’s spectral 1982 masterpiece, famously recorded on a finicky four-track cassette machine in a shag-carpeted bedroom in Colts Neck, New Jersey. In the movie’s telling, Bruce returns hollowed out from The River tour and throws himself into depressed but productive isolation, venturing outside of his rented house on the reservoir only to stare mournfully at his nearby dilapidated childhood home or rip guitar solos with a hard-rocking blues band at his old stomping grounds, The Stone Pony. There, he meets Faye (Odessa Young), the younger sister of some guy from high school, and the pair strike up a tender but increasingly emotionally fraught romance. A chance late-night TV viewing of Terence Malick’s Badlands (1973) sends him on a songwriting streak, producing everything from surefire hits like “Born in the USA” and “I’m on Fire” to the desolate, austere tales of spree killers, highway patrolmen, and nighttime drivers that would eventually populate Nebraska .

Meanwhile, Stephen Graham and Gaby Hoffmann haunt him as his parents in recurring black-and-white flashback sequences, and a scenery-chewing Jeremy Strong, playing Bruce’s manager Jon Landau, flits in and out of the film dripped out in full ’80s-sportswear regalia. In a revealing choice, Landau, an accomplished producer and critic, is presented here as a kind of cross between hype man and life coach, whose primary role is to translate Bruce’s art into corporate jargon for the suits at CBS: “In this office, my office, we believe in Bruce Springsteen.”

Deliver Me from Nowhere is not much interested in probing Springsteen the performer, and it’s even less interested in him as a songwriter. For a film whose plot essentially revolves around the writing and recording of an album, it can’t find a sincere way of imagining the everyday process of writing lyrics and making music. Instead, Cooper, who also wrote the screenplay, reaches for ham-fisted false equivalences between life and art. A scene of Bruce furiously scribbling “why?” while researching Charles Starkweather, the real-life killer who inspired Malick’s Badlands , reminded me of Jason Bourne’s clumsy attempts to uncover his past by filling notebooks with half-remembered words, drawings, and questions like “WHO WAS I?” At its worst, the film leans on a spurious one-to-one connection between Bruce’s increasingly dark and complex songs and his depression, stemming from childhood trauma, all telegraphed through the aforementioned flashback sequences—as if the meaning and potency of artistic expression could be fully explained away in terms of its creator’s mental health, and more specifically in this case, boiled down to Bruce’s relationship with his father.

Framing the songs as only being about “what Bruce is going through” also allows the film to pump up artificial drama about the music’s commercial viability or lack thereof, with Strong’s Landau running interference between Bruce’s sadness and the “real world” of record executives and studio engineers. Thus, a scene depicting Bruce and the E Street Band recording “Born in the U.S.A.” in the studio can only be about how Bruce shelves a hit record in favor of his emo bedroom music. Shockingly, no one cares to say anything at all about the content of the song itself, whose famously bleak lyrics depict an emotionally wrecked Vietnam vet returning home to an indifferent and contemptuous American society. In fact, there’s not one suggestion in the entire film that these songs have anything to do with the political or social world around him.

It’s a shame, because Nebraska is an intensely cinematic album—one that Springsteen often describes in terms of its characters, atmospheres, and spaces rather than his own personal struggle and redemption. It’s densely packed with detail and texture, a road map of a uniquely American isolation through specific place names (Lincoln, Perrineville, Mahwah), imagistic phrases (“They blew up the chicken man in Philly last night”; “I remember Wanda up on scrap metal hill”), and repeating motifs, like the radio relay and refinery towers, the debts no honest man can pay, and the spectral glow of the New Jersey Turnpike “in the wee wee hours,” looking like some “lunar landscape.”

What Springsteen found in filmic influences like Malick’s Badlands and Charles Laughton’s 1955 psychological thriller The Night of the Hunter (which Dutch Springsteen takes young Bruce to see in Deliver Me from Nowhere ) was more than a just the character model in the sociopathic American killer—it was what he called the “deadly meditative feeling of nature . . . [that] brings forth a sort of mythic dread.” He found that dread lurking just beyond the manicured front lawn of Sissy Spacek’s childhood home in Badlands and in Laughton’s famously spooky cutaway to a pair of rabbits silently keeping watch along a riverbed. This feeling comes across in the album’s dead-space tape hiss and ghostly reverb effects as much as it does in its clipped, sketch-like stories of violence, fear, and memory. Landau armchair-psychologizes at one point in the film, claiming these dark songs are really just Bruce’s personal confession of guilt and unresolved trauma. They’re a cry for help, he insists. But, as per usual, the Boss says it better, in compelling terms that expand outward rather than close in on themselves: “Everyone knows what it’s like to be condemned.”

article_text:
It has been widely reported that the Kennedy Center is at the center of a power struggle between the Trump administration and preservationists, as the president wants to rename it in his own honor and insists that the decaying building must close for renovations. He has threatened that it will be razed if he does not get his way.

Now, CNN reports that donors who have given artwork to the institution are trying to reclaim their gifts, fearing for their safety amid a renovation and in the wake of layoffs. They are not convinced that the leadership, largely appointed by Trump, values the artworks as part of the institution’s holdings.

According to an internal document reviewed by CNN, officials have been working since at least late last year on a plan that proposed the “disposal” of artworks, whether by “return to country of origin, transfer or exchange with another institution, public sale, or destruction.”

“I want to get that sculpture out of there,” one person who donated a piece told CNN.

Donors, as well as artists and their families, have been trying for months to get answers, the report says, to questions about how the artworks will be safeguarded, where they are, and whether they will be returned. Their fears were not assuaged when Trump ordered the disassembly and removal of a monumental Joel Shapiro sculpture from the institution’s grounds. The work had been gifted to the center but was sold to its former chairman, David Rubenstein. The reason for its removal has not been explained.

“We remain in regular contact with the foundations and entities who have donated art to the center,” a Kennedy Center spokesperson told CNN. But an unidentified person described as close to the Kennedy Center said the institution’s response has been “a little bit disjointed” and that donors are “not given detail in any way.”

The Kennedy Center has long been home to hundreds of unique works of art and antiquities, including sculptures and tapestries, donated or loaned by individual benefactors and other countries, CNN notes. Officials say the proposal contemplating the “destruction” of art “was never envisioned as a sweeping purge.” They told CNN that the “cornerstone of the collection—historic international gifts given to the center for its opening—remains intact.”

The Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to a request from ARTnews to clarify how much of the center’s collection falls under that “cornerstone” designation, or what circumstances would lead to the destruction of artworks.

Officials told CNN that all artwork will be “fully safeguarded” during the renovation, with some pieces relocated if necessary to ensure their safety. But sources also told CNN that objects belonging to the archives have been “inadvertently” taken home by staffers.

Following Kennedy’s assassination, world leaders rushed to donate artworks: France gave tapestries by Henri Matisse, and Tunisia gave a reproduction of a third-century mosaic for the rooftop terrace, CNN notes.

Josef Palermo, formerly the curator in charge of visual art programming, was laid off earlier this year. He wrote in an Atlantic essay that he had been instructed to begin removing artworks on view.

CNN also notes that the Kennedy Center recently convened, with no announcement, its first visual arts committee, “to curate and expand public installations of performing and visual arts.”

title_original: Dreamy work by SWANA artists on show in Perth
editorial_title_zh: 西南亚及北非艺术家的梦幻作品在珀斯展出
editorial_excerpt_zh: 2025年威康摄影奖通过跨越家庭暴力、气候移民和微观疾病等强大影像，凸显了全球健康挑战
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "汇集了来自西南亚、北非及其众多海外 diaspora（流散社群）的7位在世艺术家和一个艺术家组合的作品，《没有哪个夜晚足够漫长能让我们做两次梦》（No night is long enough for us to dream twice）在西澳大利亚美术馆呈现了一种拓展的影像创作方法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“没有哪个夜晚足够漫长能让我们做两次梦”是巴勒斯坦作家马哈茂德·达尔维什（Mahmoud Darwish）的诗作《渡鸦之墨》（The Raven’s Ink）中的名句。达尔维什1941年出生于阿尔比尔瓦（al-Birwa），1948年该村被以色列国防军攻占并夷为平地，他和家人被迫逃离；这家人设法搬回了附近，但由于错过了以色列的人口普查，被归类为“在场-缺席的外侨”。达尔维什觉得这种处境十分荒谬，并在诗歌中运用荒诞主义和超现实主义来表达流亡的破碎现实。但他同时也用它们来构想新的可能性。诗人娜奥米·谢哈布·奈（Naomi Shihab Nye）曾说，他的诗“富有抒情性、意象感、哀怨、萦绕心头、始终充满激情与优雅——而且永远绝对自由——这是他为他所有的人民所梦想的”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "策展人达利娅·阿尔-杜贾伊利（Dalia Al-Dujaili）在筹备于西澳大利亚美术馆展出至31日的展览《没有哪个夜晚足够漫长能让我们做两次梦》时，深受达尔维什创作实践的启发；她与联合策展人雷切尔·谢斯瓦（Rachel Cieśla）一起，将来自SWANA（西南亚及北非）地区及其流散社群艺术家的作品汇集在一起，希望超越这一地区常见的那种纪实影像，走向更具解放性的方向。“我很想探索地区和流散SWANA艺术家如何利用荒诞主义和超现实主义等艺术流派与哲学方法来拓展摄影的可能性，”她解释道，“我们地区的很多作品都局限于战争或纪实美学与方法，虽然在某些语境下有用，但它让人感觉扁平、非人化，同时也限制了这些摄影师的艺术生涯。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我还觉得，欧洲中心主义的策展方法强加了这种美学，他们来看关于SWANA的展览时，往往带着对某种特定情绪或愿景的预期，而这正是我真正想要挑战的。我对国旗、石榴以及这些英雄式的解放影像并不感兴趣——尽管它们在其他语境中同样非常美丽。我希望观众对游戏、欲望、色欲、暴力和庆祝等概念的普遍性感到惊讶，以及当这些概念在相机镜头发下受到审视时，它们是如何在这个地区上演的。”", "translated": 的艺术家纳入其中，他们的影像既受到距离的塑造，也受到他们出身之地的塑造。相反，吸引我们的并非某种共同地理之外的东西——而是一种与压力的关联，”她继续说道，“他们每个人都在社会力量不断积聚、破裂又重新积聚的空间内创作影像，无论是城市、家园还是身体。将它们并置在一起，能让你看到这种压力在不同语境下如何以不同方式显现，以及它们之间究竟产生了怎样的共鸣。”", "translated": true}, article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Gathering work by seven living artists and one artist duo from across South West Asia, North Africa, and its many diasporas, No night is long enough for us to dream twice presents an expanded approach to image-making at the Art Gallery of Western Australia"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“No night is long enough for us to dream twice” is a celebrated line from the poem The Raven’s Ink, by Palestinian author Mahmoud Darwish. Born in al-Birwa in 1941, Darwish was forced to flee the village with his family in 1948, when it was captured and razed by the Israel Defense Forces; the family managed to return to close nearby but, having missed the Israeli census, was assigned ‘present-absent aliens’. Darwish found this situation absurd, and he used absurdism and surrealism in his poems to articulate the fragmented reality of exile. But he also used them to envisage new possibilities. His poems are “lyrical, imagistic, plaintive, haunting, always passionate and elegant – and never anything less than free – what he would dream for all his people”, poet Naomi Shihab Nye has said."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Curator Dalia Al-Dujaili was inspired by Darwish’s practice when working on the exhibition No night is long enough for us to dream twice , on show at The Art Gallery of Western Australia until 31 January; putting together work by artists from across the SWANA region and its diaspora with co-curator Rachel Cieśla, she wanted to reach beyond the documentary imagery so often seen from this area, and towards something more liberatory. “I was curious to explore how regional and diaspora SWANA artists utilise artistic movements and philosophical approaches such as absurdism and surrealism to expand the possibility of photography,” she explains. “So much of the work from our region is stuck in war or documentary aesthetics and approaches, and whilst useful in some contexts, it feels flattening, dehumanising and also limiting for the artistic careers of these photographers."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I also feel like Eurocentric curatorial approaches impose these kinds of aesthetics and want to go to shows about the SWANA expecting a certain kind of mood or vision, which I really wanted to challenge. I was not interested in flags and pomegranates and these heroic images of liberation – though, again, so beautiful in other contexts. I wanted audiences to be surprised by the universality of concepts like play, desire, lust, violence and celebration and how these play out in the region when they are scrutinised under the camera lens.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The idea I’ve been working with is ‘documentary futurity’: a documentary impulse that records what is happening while also imagining what could come next,” adds Cieśla. “Dreaming is the right word for that, because a dream isn’t a record of the past. It’s the mind opening out onto another world that I’ve created in order to try out another possibility. In the exhibition, you see photographs and videos that stay with difficult sites without settling into elegy. They keep a door open.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/8.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Hicham Benohoud, Untitled from the series 'La Salle de Classe’, 1994-2000, archival pigment print © Hicham Benohoud. Courtesy of the Artist", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Basel-Abbas-and-Ruanne-Abou-Rahme-still-from-Collapse-2009-3.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Basel Abbas and Ruanne Abou-Rahme, Collapse, 2009 (still) © Basel Abbas and Ruanne Abou-Rahme. Courtesy the artists", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "quote", "text": "“The idea I’ve been working with is ‘documentary futurity’: a documentary impulse that records what is happening while also imagining what could come next.” Rachel Cieśla"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "No night is long enough for us to dream twice includes seven living artists and one artist duo whose work opens this sense of possibility; the artists span the South West Asia North Africa region, including Algeria, Iran, Lebanon, Morocco, Palestine, and Türkiye. The exhibition includes a site-specific new iteration of Abdulhamid Kircher’s Rotting from within (2026), which includes photographs, family snaps, and 30 video works to create a dense collage, seemingly at the edge of what it can contain. Describing Kircher’s relationship with his estranged father, Rotting from within includes moments of peace and love, all the joy and pain of what the curators describe as “the unruly complexity of lived experience”."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Lebanese image-maker Mohamad Abdouni considers family alongside intimacy and queer experience, in which images become inseparable from questions of belonging and visibility; Hicham Benohoud – who hails from a different generation – embraces a different kind of messy with his portraits of Moroccan school children, taken while he was an art teacher. article_text:
Gathering work by seven living artists and one artist duo from across South West Asia, North Africa, and its many diasporas, No night is long enough for us to dream twice presents an expanded approach to image-making at the Art Gallery of Western Australia

“No night is long enough for us to dream twice” is a celebrated line from the poem The Raven’s Ink, by Palestinian author Mahmoud Darwish. Born in al-Birwa in 1941, Darwish was forced to flee the village with his family in 1948, when it was captured and razed by the Israel Defense Forces; the family managed to return to close nearby but, having missed the Israeli census, was assigned ‘present-absent aliens’. Darwish found this situation absurd, and he used absurdism and surrealism in his poems to articulate the fragmented reality of exile. But he also used them to envisage new possibilities. His poems are “lyrical, imagistic, plaintive, haunting, always passionate and elegant – and never anything less than free – what he would dream for all his people”, poet Naomi Shihab Nye has said.

Curator Dalia Al-Dujaili was inspired by Darwish’s practice when working on the exhibition No night is long enough for us to dream twice , on show at The Art Gallery of Western Australia until 31 January; putting together work by artists from across the SWANA region and its diaspora with co-curator Rachel Cieśla, she wanted to reach beyond the documentary imagery so often seen from this area, and towards something more liberatory. “I was curious to explore how regional and diaspora SWANA artists utilise artistic movements and philosophical approaches such as absurdism and surrealism to expand the possibility of photography,” she explains. “So much of the work from our region is stuck in war or documentary aesthetics and approaches, and whilst useful in some contexts, it feels flattening, dehumanising and also limiting for the artistic careers of these photographers.

“I also feel like Eurocentric curatorial approaches impose these kinds of aesthetics and want to go to shows about the SWANA expecting a certain kind of mood or vision, which I really wanted to challenge. I was not interested in flags and pomegranates and these heroic images of liberation – though, again, so beautiful in other contexts. I wanted audiences to be surprised by the universality of concepts like play, desire, lust, violence and celebration and how these play out in the region when they are scrutinised under the camera lens.”

“The idea I’ve been working with is ‘documentary futurity’: a documentary impulse that records what is happening while also imagining what could come next,” adds Cieśla. “Dreaming is the right word for that, because a dream isn’t a record of the past. It’s the mind opening out onto another world that I’ve created in order to try out another possibility. In the exhibition, you see photographs and videos that stay with difficult sites without settling into elegy. They keep a door open.”

“The idea I’ve been working with is ‘documentary futurity’: a documentary impulse that records what is happening while also imagining what could come next.” Rachel Cieśla

No night is long enough for us to dream twice includes seven living artists and one artist duo whose work opens this sense of possibility; the artists span the South West Asia North Africa region, including Algeria, Iran, Lebanon, Morocco, Palestine, and Türkiye. The exhibition includes a site-specific new iteration of Abdulhamid Kircher’s Rotting from within (2026), which includes photographs, family snaps, and 30 video works to create a dense collage, seemingly at the edge of what it can contain. Describing Kircher’s relationship with his estranged father, Rotting from within includes moments of peace and love, all the joy and pain of what the curators describe as “the unruly complexity of lived experience”.

Lebanese image-maker Mohamad Abdouni considers family alongside intimacy and queer experience, in which images become inseparable from questions of belonging and visibility; Hicham Benohoud – who hails from a different generation – embraces a different kind of messy with his portraits of Moroccan school children, taken while he was an art teacher. Disillusioned with the rigid four-hour lessons he was expected to run, Benohoud transformed his classroom into a studio in which the students could be creatively free. Photographing the results between 1994-2002, his images are warm and anarchic; they also imply a critique of the education system, and what Benohoud saw as its failings.

Sabiha Çimen explores life for school kids too, her series Hafiz shot in girls-only Qur’an schools in Turkey; finding moments of humour and intimacy, it speaks of rich inner lives inside the uniforms. Born in Istanbul, Çimen is a self-taught photographer and now a member of Magnum Photos; Hafiz was her first photobook, and it won the 2022 Paris Photo-Aperture First PhotoBook award. No night is long enough for us to dream twice also includes important projects by Myriam Boulos and Hannah Darabi, both of whom explore intimacy and sexuality amid times of protest and political change; Boulos is from Lebanon, and is also a member of Magnum Photos, while Darabi uses found images to talk of Iran. Darabi’s Why Don’t You Dance? used collage as a means to discuss bodily autonomy and personal liberation; No night is long enough for us to dream twice includes a satirical 1980s gym dance class, which Darabi shot as a video work.

The exhibition also includes two other video works. Basel Abbas and Ruanne Abou-Rahme, who are of Palestinian descent, contribute the video-sound installation Collapse, which combines original documentary and material from historic films and “leads you into the slightly darker moments of the show”; Mohamed Bourouissa, the Algerian-born French photographer, shows his video work Généalogie de la Violence (Genealogy of Violence), 2024, in which a young couple in a car chat and discuss their future – until they are interrupted by a police identity check. Bourouissa is also exhibiting his seminal image Le cercle imaginaire (2007-08), from broader work Périphérique , which investigates social tensions in the marginalised Parisian banlieues.

Darabi’s film is being shown on an appropriately retro 1980s TV, but the two other films are being shown at large scale, as are many of the images, and Kircher’s whole-wall installation. “We blew a lot of the images up because we wanted the show to feel really immersive,” Al-Dujaili explains. “I talk about it like walking through a fever dream.” She and Cieśla have also included a book display to help add context though; the audience in Perth won’t necessarily have much knowledge or understanding of the richness of SWANA-region photography, Al-Dujaili points out, so they wanted to help them get acquainted. “It felt important to challenge what these audiences might expect walking into a SWANA show, and hopefully they will leave with a new ‘to read’ list or a new photobook in their hands.”

And it was books that brought Al-Dujaili and Cieśla together, and helped bring the show into being; Cieśla heard about Al-Dujaili through her HIKMA project – an online repository and library for materials on Mesopotamia and modern day Iraq – and reached out to her via WhatsApp. Their shared interest in photography from the SWANA region and its diaspora soon became clear, and evolved into the idea of an exhibition around this work and the theme of dreams. Cieśla is Lead Creative at The Simon Lee Foundation Institute of Contemporary Asian Art, a curatorial initiative at The Art Gallery of Western Australia which she describes as “working to enrich AGWA’s connections with contemporary artists and cultural thinking in Asia and across its diasporas”. The Institute is wary of shows that are geographically bounded in a fixed sense, she adds, so No night is long enough for us to dream twice is deliberately wide, including artists from across the region and its diaspora rather than honing in on a particular culture.

This approach is also appropriate, she adds, reflecting its geographical, political and cultural history. “The borders across SWANA have been drawn and redrawn, and people move across them constantly, through exile, migration and family ties. A show built around one place might have treated those lines as fixed, when for many of these artists they aren’t. It also meant we could include artists working in the diaspora, whose images are shaped by distance as much as by where they come from. What we were drawn to instead was something these artists share beyond a common geography – a relation to pressure,” she continues. “Each of them makes images within spaces where social forces are building, breaking and building again, whether that’s a city, a home, or a body. Putting them side-by-side lets you see how that pressure shows up differently in each context, and what echoes between them anyway.”

No night is long enough for us to dream twice is on show at The Art Gallery of Western Australia until 31 January 2027 artgallery.wa.gov.au

article_text:
「鴨居玲―カメラが捉えた画家の素顔―」が 12 月 20 日まで、茨城県の笠間日動美術館で開かれています。（敬称略）

鴨居玲（ 1928-1985） は「自画像の画家」と呼ばれ、作品には自身の内面が表現され、見るものの感情を揺さぶります。一方、作品からは見えてこない＜人間＞としての鴨居玲も存在します。本展では、同美術館所蔵作品約70点に加え、鴨居と晩年の約 15 年間をともにしたパートナーで写真家の富山栄美子(1941-)が残した貴重なポートレートを中心に写真約 75 点を展示して、鴨居の素顔を探ります。

富山は 1941 年、ロシア人を父、日本人を母として、東京で生まれました。女子美術大学付属高校から写真の専門学校に進み、スポーツニッポンのカメラマンになりました。その後、各国を回って写真を撮っていましたが、 38 歳の鴨居とフランスで出会います。鴨居が新人の登竜門である安井賞を受けた 1969 年にパリで再会。 1971 年からスペインのマドリードで生活を共にして、 1977 年に帰国後も鴨居が自死した 1985 年まで生涯をともにしました。

2015 年以降、富山は同館に、鴨居の絵画、家具、愛用品のほか、鴨居を撮影した多数の写真を託しました。今回は、鴨居の絵だけではなく、多くの未公開写真を展示している点がユニークです。

展覧会は５章構成で、序章「一期は夢よ」では、少年期から 1969 年に安井賞と昭和会優秀賞を受賞するまでの、恩師・宮本三郎の影響が残る作品を中心に展示しています。

１章「私の小さな村」ではスペインとフランス時代の作品が集められています。スペイン時代は、おじいさんやおばあさんなどのモチーフを描いた非常に素晴らしい時期になります。

２章「何故、自分は『神』を持っていないのか」は、人間以外でシリーズ化した教会シリーズが並びます。

3 章の「神戸日記」は、 1977 年に帰国した神戸で、裸婦のほか、自画像や首吊りなどをテーマに描いた作品が並びます。裸婦については、交流の深かった長谷川徳七・名誉館長が、鴨居のシャイさを表すエピソードを紹介してくれました。鴨居はスペイン時代、おじいさんやおばあさん、傷病兵とか画題には事欠くことがありませんでした。しかし、日本に帰るとそういう人々が見当たらず、「先生、女性、特に裸婦を描いたらどうですか」と勧めたそうです。「ただ先生は非常に恥ずかしがり屋で、うまく描くことができなかった」と振り返ります。愛し合った二人が抱き合って最後に石になるというテーマのロシア映画「石の花」をモティーフにしてから、だんだんと慣れて描けるようになったそうです。「それでも、後ろ向きの裸婦が非常に多く、前向きはほとんど描かなかった」と長谷川名誉館長は付け加えました。

終章「憂きことも嬉しいことも」では、富山が撮影した貴重な写真を中心に、交友やプライベートの姿を紹介しています。特に体重80㎏を超えるセントバーナードの愛犬チータと、子どものような笑顔でじゃれ合っている姿は、作風からからは思いもつきません。自身は子どもを持ちませんでしたが、スペインの子どもと親子のように入浴する写真は印象的です。

また、トレードマークであるサングラスや派手なジャケットなど貴重な小物はファンならずとも興味を引かれるでしょう。

ほかにフォトスポットも充実していて、絶筆の自画像がかかったアトリエを訪れたり、名作《私の話を聞いてくれ》の前でおじいさんと話し合う写真なども撮影できます。ほかに、作品や資料、大切に使っていたアンティーク家具や身の回りの愛用品などを展示している常設の「鴨居玲の部屋」もあります。

長谷川智恵子・副館長は「いわゆる美男子は冷たい感じの方が多いと思うんですけれども、彼は温かい人でした。周りに来る友達を楽しんで見守っているタイプでした。私たちはたくさんの絵描きさんとお付き合いがありますが、鴨居さんとの交流はたった 17 年間でした。それでも、パリでも神戸でもスペインでも一緒に楽しく飲みました。だから、とってもいい思い出があって、そういう意味では鴨居先生はすごく身近で、いつまでも私の心の中に生きている。そんな感じのする作家です」と振り返ります。

人間の内面に潜む弱さや孤独、絶望を強烈な筆致で描いた鴨居玲。本展は、そんな作家がイヌや子どもたちと無邪気に戯れる様子を、心を許したパートナーの写真家が切り取った貴重な一面を私たちに見せてくれます。（美術展ナビ編集班・若水浩）

鴨居玲―カメラが捉えた画家の素顔―
